ep.Question: A historian notices that peasants still paid rent to a landowner after the Black Death, but now in money rather than labour. Which historical concept best describes this observation?
ep.Option A: Contestability
ep.Option B: Continuity and change
ep.Option C: Empathy
ep.Feedback shown to students: Something stayed the same (rent) while its form changed (money instead of labour). That is continuity and change working together.
ep.Teacher notes: Applies the concept rather than asking for the definition. Tests the most-confused pair.

ep.Question: Two textbooks disagree about whether Commodore Perry's arrival or internal problems did more to end the Tokugawa shogunate. Which historical concept does this disagreement illustrate?
ep.Option A: Contestability
ep.Option B: Cause and effect
ep.Option C: Significance
ep.Feedback shown to students: When historians interpret the same past differently, the interpretation is contestable. The disagreement is about causes, but the concept describing a disagreement itself is contestability.

ep.Question:
Complete the passage.
Historians judge the [significance] of an event by asking how many people it affected, how deeply it changed their lives and how long the change lasted. To understand why people acted as they did without judging them by today's standards, historians use [empathy]. The clues gathered from a source by asking questions of it are called [evidence].
ep.Option A: Blank 1 options: significance / perspective / contestability
ep.Option B: Blank 2 options: empathy / evidence / continuity
ep.Option C: Blank 3 options: evidence / sources / facts
ep.Feedback shown to students: Significance is judged by scale, depth and duration. Empathy is understanding people in their own context. Evidence is what you draw out of a source, not the source itself.

ep.Stimulus (text to paste as text stimulus: Source caption. Adapted from the Decameron by Giovanni Boccaccio, written in Florence, Italy, c. 1350.
ep.Question: In which century was this source created?
ep.Option A: 12th century
ep.Option B: 13th century
ep.Option C: 14th century
ep.Feedback shown to students: 1350 falls in the 1300s, which is the 14th century. Add one to the hundreds digit to find the century.
ep.Teacher notes: Students repeatedly lose the century question. Pair with a Japan version.

ep.Stimulus (text to paste as text stimulus: Source caption. Woodblock print by Katsushika Hokusai, produced in Edo, Japan, 1831.
ep.Question: What is the origin of this source?
ep.Option A: A Japanese artist working in the 17th century
ep.Option B: A Japanese artist working in the 19th century
ep.Option C: A European traveller visiting Japan in the 18th century
ep.Option D: A Japanese official writing in the Meiji period
ep.Feedback shown to students: Origin means who made it, where and when. 1831 is the 19th century and Edo was the shogun's capital, so this was made inside Tokugawa Japan before Perry arrived in 1853.

ep.Stimulus (text to paste as text stimulus: Source caption. Wall painting of the Last Judgement showing demons dragging sinners into hell, painted inside a village church in England, c. 1400. Most villagers could not read.
ep.Question: Using COMA, what was the most likely purpose of this painting?
ep.Option A: To decorate the church so that wealthy visitors would donate money
ep.Option B: To record an actual event that the villagers had witnessed
ep.Option C: To teach an audience that could not read what the Church said would happen to sinners
ep.Option D: To criticise the priests who ran the church
ep.Feedback shown to students: Content (hell), origin (inside a church), audience (villagers who could not read). Put together, the message was a visual warning about sin that reinforced the Church's authority.

ep.Stimulus (text to paste as text stimulus:
Adapted from a letter by a European merchant visiting Nagasaki, 1640s.
"Only the Dutch and the Chinese may now trade here, and only on the small island built for them in the harbour. No Japanese ship may sail abroad and any Japanese who has lived overseas is forbidden to return. The missionaries have all been expelled and the Christian faith is outlawed on pain of death."
ep.Question: Highlight the TWO phrases that give evidence that sakoku restricted the movement of Japanese people, not only foreigners.
ep.Correct answer: No Japanese ship may sail abroad; any Japanese who has lived overseas is forbidden to return
ep.Feedback shown to students: Sakoku worked in both directions. The source shows restrictions on foreigners (Dutch and Chinese only, one island) and on Japanese (no sailing abroad, no return). The two highlighted phrases are the evidence for the second part.
ep.Teacher notes: EP Highlight question. Students select words in the passage. Set the two target phrases as correct.

ep.Exam skill or knowledge tested: Read a timeline and order events
ep.Question:
Put these events in order by choosing the correct event for each position.
Earliest [Battle of Hastings, 1066] then [First Crusade begins, 1096] then [Genpei War ends and Minamoto Yoritomo becomes shogun, 1192] then [Black Death reaches Europe, 1347] then [Battle of Sekigahara, 1600] then [Commodore Perry arrives in Japan, 1853].
ep.Option A: Each blank offers all six events as dropdown options
ep.Correct answer: Hastings 1066; First Crusade 1096; Yoritomo shogun 1192; Black Death 1347; Sekigahara 1600; Perry 1853
ep.Feedback shown to students: The two units overlap in time. The first shogun ruled a century after Hastings and the Black Death struck Europe while the Kamakura shogunate was in power in Japan.
ep.Teacher notes: EP has no ordering question. Use fill the gaps with a dropdown at each position and the same six options in every dropdown. Dates are removed in the student view if you want it harder.

ep.Exam skill or knowledge tested: Read a timeline and order events
ep.Question: Which of the following happened in Japan while the Black Death was spreading through Europe in the late 1340s?
ep.Option A: The Tokugawa shogunate was enforcing sakoku
ep.Option B: The Kamakura shogunate had recently fallen and the Ashikaga shoguns held power
ep.Option C: Emperor Meiji was modernising the army
ep.Option D: The Genpei War was being fought
ep.Feedback shown to students: The Kamakura shogunate ended in 1333 and the Ashikaga (Muromachi) shogunate began in 1336, so this is the period that overlaps with the Black Death. Sakoku and Meiji are centuries later, and the Genpei War was 150 years earlier.

ep.Question: Which statement gives the strongest reason for calling the Battle of Sekigahara (1600) a turning point?
ep.Option A: It was the largest battle in Japanese history
ep.Option B: Many samurai died on both sides
ep.Option C: It ended more than a century of civil war and allowed Tokugawa Ieyasu to establish a shogunate that ruled for over 250 years
ep.Option D: It was fought near Kyoto, the home of the emperor
ep.Feedback shown to students: A turning point changes the direction of history. Size, casualties and location are details. The long-term consequence (Tokugawa rule and 250 years of peace) is what makes it a turning point.
ep.Teacher notes: Distractors are true facts that are not reasons. Trains students to separate description from significance, the gap the moderation notes flagged.

ep.Exam skill or knowledge tested: Key features of the feudal system
ep.Question: Which exchange best describes the agreement at the heart of European feudalism?
ep.Option A: The Church gave land to kings in return for tithes
ep.Option B: A lord granted a fief to a vassal in return for loyalty and military service
ep.Option C: Peasants paid money to knights in return for weapons
ep.Option D: Merchants gave goods to nobles in return for titles
ep.Feedback shown to students: Feudalism was built on land for service. The lord gave a fief (land) and the vassal gave loyalty and service, usually as a knight.

ep.Question:
Complete the hierarchy from the top down.
The [monarch] owned all the land and granted large estates to the [nobles], who in turn gave smaller fiefs to [knights] in return for military service. At the bottom, [peasants] farmed the land and gave a share of their produce to the lord of the manor.
ep.Option A: Each blank offers: monarch / nobles / knights / peasants / clergy
ep.Feedback shown to students: Land flowed downwards and service flowed upwards. The clergy sat alongside this structure rather than inside it, which is why it is the distractor.

ep.Question: What was the main difference between a serf and a free peasant?
ep.Option A: Serfs were paid in coins while free peasants were paid in food
ep.Option B: Serfs were bound to their lord's land and could not leave without permission, while free peasants could move
ep.Option C: Serfs lived in towns while free peasants lived on manors
ep.Option D: Serfs could become knights but free peasants could not
ep.Feedback shown to students: A serf was tied to the manor and owed labour to the lord. Freedom of movement was the key difference, and it is why the labour shortage after the Black Death mattered so much to serfs.

ep.Question: Why did feudalism help a medieval king keep control of a large kingdom without a modern army or police force?
ep.Option A: Every subject swore an oath directly to the king
ep.Option B: Nobles who held land from the king were obliged to supply knights and keep order in their own regions
ep.Option C: The Church forced peasants to obey the king
ep.Option D: Kings employed professional soldiers paid from taxes
ep.Feedback shown to students: The king could not govern everywhere at once. Granting land to nobles made them responsible for defending and controlling their region, in return for their oath of loyalty.

ep.Question: What is the name for the land a lord granted to a vassal in return for loyalty and service? (one word)
ep.Feedback shown to students: A fief was the land itself. The vassal was the person who received it.
ep.Teacher notes: EP Textbox. Add alternative accepted answers: fief, Fief, feif (common misspelling, your call).

ep.Question: True or false. A vassal was always a knight.
ep.Option A: True
ep.Option B: False
ep.Feedback shown to students: A vassal was anyone who swore loyalty to a lord in return for land or protection. Nobles were vassals of the king, and knights were vassals of nobles. The word describes the relationship, not the job.

ep.Question: Which TWO of the following were expectations of a knight under the code of chivalry?
ep.Option A: Protect the weak and defenceless
ep.Option B: Accumulate as much land as possible
ep.Option C: Show loyalty to his lord
ep.Option D: Avoid all combat unless ordered by the Church
ep.Feedback shown to students: Chivalry demanded courage, loyalty, protection of the weak, courtesy and devotion to the Church. Gaining land was a reward, not a rule, and knights were expected to fight.

ep.Question: A European knight and a Japanese samurai were similar in that both...
ep.Option A: were paid a salary by the central government
ep.Option B: were warriors who served a lord in return for land or income and followed a code of conduct
ep.Option C: were elected by the peasants they protected
ep.Option D: were forbidden to own weapons in peacetime
ep.Feedback shown to students: Both were warrior classes bound by loyalty to a lord, rewarded with land or a stipend, and guided by a code (chivalry or bushido). The differences lie in religion, the role of the emperor and the detail of the codes.
ep.Teacher notes: Prepares for the compare-style short answer.

ep.Question: A peasant and a noble living on the same manor in 1250 would most likely have had different perspectives on feudalism because...
ep.Option A: they spoke different languages
ep.Option B: the system gave the noble protection and wealth while it gave the peasant protection but demanded labour and limited freedom
ep.Option C: the noble was not part of the feudal system
ep.Feedback shown to students: Perspective depends on position in society. The same system looked like security and status from the top and like obligation from the bottom.

ep.Question: Which development did the most to weaken feudalism in the later Middle Ages?
ep.Option A: The invention of the printing press
ep.Option B: The growth of towns, trade and a money economy alongside the labour shortage after the Black Death
ep.Option C: The First Crusade
ep.Feedback shown to students: When labour became scarce and money more common, peasants could demand wages or leave for towns. Lords lost their grip on the land-for-labour bargain.
ep.Teacher notes: Links the three Medieval Europe topics together.

ep.Question: Why were most punishments in medieval Europe carried out in public, in the market square or at the town gate?
ep.Option A: Because prisons were full
ep.Option B: To shame the offender and warn others, since there was no police force and fear was the main deterrent
ep.Option C: So the king could watch personally
ep.Option D: To raise money by selling tickets
ep.Feedback shown to students: With no police, order depended on deterrence. Stocks, pillories and executions were public so that the whole community saw the consequences of breaking the law.

ep.Question:
Match each crime to its likely medieval punishment.
A baker who sold underweight loaves might be put in the [stocks or pillory]. A peasant caught poaching deer in the lord's forest could face [a fine, mutilation or hanging]. A noble found guilty of treason against the king faced [execution and loss of all property]. A person accused of heresy could be [excommunicated or burned at the stake].
ep.Option A: Each blank offers all four punishments
ep.Correct answer: stocks or pillory; a fine, mutilation or hanging; execution and loss of all property; excommunicated or burned at the stake
ep.Feedback shown to students: Punishments matched the seriousness of the crime and who was offended. Cheating customers was a public nuisance, poaching stole from the lord, treason attacked the king and heresy attacked the Church.

ep.Question: In a trial by ordeal, an accused person might carry a red-hot iron and have the wound inspected three days later. What belief made this seem a fair way to decide guilt?
ep.Option A: That burns always heal in three days
ep.Option B: That God would protect the innocent and reveal the guilty through the outcome
ep.Option C: That the lord could tell liars by their faces
ep.Feedback shown to students: Medieval justice assumed God intervened in the world. The ordeal was a way of asking God for a verdict. Trial by jury of local men gradually replaced it after the Church withdrew support in 1215.

ep.Question: Which statement best explains the Church's role in medieval law and order?
ep.Option A: The Church had no part in legal matters
ep.Option B: The Church ran its own courts under canon law, judged crimes such as heresy, and its threat of excommunication and hell shaped how people behaved
ep.Option C: The Church only punished priests
ep.Option D: The Church replaced the king's courts entirely
ep.Feedback shown to students: Two systems ran side by side. The king's courts handled most crime, while Church courts applied canon law to clergy, marriage, wills and belief. Fear of damnation was itself a form of social control.

ep.Question: What is the term for a crime that involves betraying or plotting against the king? (one word)
ep.Feedback shown to students: Treason was the most serious crime against the state and was punished by death and the loss of the offender's property.
ep.Teacher notes: EP Textbox. Accept treason and Treason.

ep.Question: Why were castles significant to power and authority in medieval Europe, beyond their use in battle?
ep.Option A: They were the only buildings that could store grain
ep.Option B: They were a visible symbol of the lord's power, a centre for collecting taxes and administering justice, and a base from which to control the surrounding land
ep.Option C: They were built to house peasants
ep.Option D: They were used mainly as churches
ep.Feedback shown to students: A castle said who ruled the area. The lord's court, treasury and garrison were inside it, and its sheer size reminded everyone of the hierarchy.

ep.Question: How did castle design change between the 11th and 13th centuries?
ep.Option A: Castles became smaller and made of wood
ep.Option B: Simple wooden motte-and-bailey castles were replaced by stone keeps and then concentric stone castles with multiple walls and towers
ep.Option C: Castles were abandoned for cities
ep.Feedback shown to students: Stone resisted fire and siege engines. Concentric designs forced attackers through several layers of defence. This is continuity and change in action, as the purpose stayed the same while the form evolved.

ep.Question: Which TWO expectations were part of the knight's code of chivalry?
ep.Option A: Fight bravely and never show cowardice
ep.Option B: Treat all peasants as equals
ep.Option C: Defend the Church and the Christian faith
ep.Feedback shown to students: Chivalry combined military courage, loyalty to lord, service to the Church and courtesy, especially towards noblewomen. It did not extend equality to peasants, who knights often treated harshly.

ep.Question: A chronicle written by a monk praises a knight for his chivalry, while a peasant's village was burned by the same knight during a war. What does this tell a historian?
ep.Option A: The monk was lying
ep.Option B: Chivalry was an ideal that governed how knights treated other nobles and the Church, and different groups experienced knights very differently
ep.Option C: Peasants did not exist in that region
ep.Option D: The knight was not a real knight
ep.Feedback shown to students: Sources reflect perspective. The code protected the knight's own class. Contrasting sources let historians see the gap between the ideal and the reality.

ep.Question: What purpose did tournaments serve for medieval knights?
ep.Option A: They were a way of farming land
ep.Option B: They provided training for war and a public stage to display skill and win status, reputation and prizes
ep.Option C: They were religious festivals run by the Church
ep.Option D: They decided who would become king
ep.Feedback shown to students: Tournaments were practice, sport and advertisement in one. A knight's reputation, and therefore his prospects of land and marriage, could be made in the lists.

ep.Question: Which TWO show how the Catholic Church influenced the everyday life of an ordinary medieval villager?
ep.Option A: The village year was organised around Church festivals and holy days, and every major life event, from baptism to burial, happened in the church
ep.Option B: Villagers elected the Pope
ep.Option C: Villagers paid a tithe of one tenth of their produce to the Church
ep.Option D: The Church ran the king's army
ep.Feedback shown to students: The Church was present at birth, marriage and death, set the calendar and took a share of every harvest. Its reach into daily life was greater than the king's.

ep.Question:
Complete the hierarchy of the clergy from the top down.
The [Pope] in Rome was head of the Church. Below him, [bishops] oversaw large regions called dioceses from their cathedrals. In each village, a [priest] conducted mass and heard confession. [Monks and nuns] lived apart in monasteries and convents, praying, copying books and caring for the sick.
ep.Option A: Each blank offers: Pope / bishops / priest / Monks and nuns / cardinals
ep.Correct answer: Pope; bishops; priest; Monks and nuns
ep.Feedback shown to students: The Church had its own hierarchy running parallel to the feudal one, with its own courts, taxes and lands. Bishops were often as powerful as nobles.

ep.Question: Which statement best explains why the Catholic Church was so powerful in medieval Europe?
ep.Option A: It had the largest army
ep.Option B: It controlled the path to heaven in a society where almost everyone believed in hell, and it also owned vast lands and collected tithes
ep.Option C: The Pope was also the king of England
ep.Feedback shown to students: Spiritual power was the foundation. Fear of damnation and the Church's monopoly on the sacraments gave it authority over kings and peasants alike. Land and wealth reinforced it.

ep.Question: How could the Pope put pressure on a king who defied him?
ep.Option A: By sending the Crusaders to attack the king
ep.Option B: By excommunicating the king, which cut him off from the Church and gave his subjects and rivals a reason to disobey him
ep.Option C: By raising the king's taxes
ep.Feedback shown to students: Excommunication was a political weapon. A king outside the Church risked losing the loyalty of nobles who feared for their own souls. Several kings backed down rather than face it.

ep.Question: Which of these shows the Church's CULTURAL power rather than its political or economic power?
ep.Option A: Owning about one third of the land in Europe
ep.Option B: Monasteries preserving and copying books, running schools and producing most of the art and architecture of the period
ep.Option C: Excommunicating a king
ep.Feedback shown to students: Political power is about control of rulers, economic power is about land and money, cultural power is about ideas, learning and art. The Church was dominant in all three, and the exam asks students to tell them apart.

ep.Question: What is the name of the religious punishment that cut a person off from the Church and its sacraments? (one word)
ep.Feedback shown to students: Excommunication meant no confession, no communion and, people believed, no entry to heaven. It was feared by kings and peasants alike.
ep.Teacher notes: EP Textbox. Accept excommunication and Excommunication.

ep.Question: True or false. The power of the Catholic Church remained unchanged throughout the medieval period.
ep.Option A: True
ep.Option B: False
ep.Feedback shown to students: Church power grew through the Crusades and the 12th and 13th centuries, then was shaken by the Black Death, when it could not stop the plague and lost many clergy. Historians look for both continuity and change.

ep.Question: What was the main stated aim of the First Crusade in 1096?
ep.Option A: To conquer Spain for the Pope
ep.Option B: To capture Jerusalem and the Holy Land from Muslim rule and protect Christian pilgrims
ep.Option C: To destroy the Byzantine Empire
ep.Option D: To open a trade route to India
ep.Feedback shown to students: Pope Urban II called on Christians to recover Jerusalem and aid the Byzantine emperor. Trade and land became consequences and motives for some, but the stated aim was religious.

ep.Stimulus (text to paste as text stimulus:
Adapted from Pope Urban II's speech at Clermont, 1095, as recorded by Robert the Monk.
"A foreign people has invaded the lands of the Christians in the East and destroyed the churches of God. Whoever goes to free the holy city will have all his sins forgiven. Let those who have been robbers now become soldiers of Christ. Let those who once fought their brothers now fight the enemies of God."
ep.Question: Highlight the phrase that shows the Pope offered a religious reward to those who joined the Crusade.
ep.Correct answer: will have all his sins forgiven
ep.Feedback shown to students: The promise of forgiveness of sins was a powerful motive in a society that feared hell. The other sentences give reasons (churches destroyed) and redirect knightly violence, but only this phrase is the reward.

ep.Question: How would a Muslim living in Jerusalem in 1099 most likely have described the arrival of the Crusaders?
ep.Option A: As the return of rightful rulers
ep.Option B: As a violent foreign invasion of a city that had been under Muslim rule for over 400 years
ep.Option C: As a peaceful religious pilgrimage
ep.Option D: As a trade mission from Italy
ep.Feedback shown to students: Perspectives differ by position. To Crusaders this was liberation. To the city's Muslim and Jewish inhabitants, many of whom were killed when the city fell, it was conquest.

ep.Question: How did the Crusades strengthen the power of the Catholic Church in the short term?
ep.Option A: The Pope gained direct control of all European armies
ep.Option B: The Pope showed he could call thousands of knights and kings to war, and the Church gained wealth and land from those who left
ep.Option C: The Church abolished feudalism
ep.Feedback shown to students: Only the Pope could unite rulers across Europe behind one cause. Crusaders also mortgaged or donated land to the Church before leaving, increasing its wealth.

ep.Question: Which TWO of these were consequences of the Crusades for Europe?
ep.Option A: Increased trade with the East, bringing goods such as spices, silk and sugar
ep.Option B: The end of the Catholic Church
ep.Option C: New knowledge from the Islamic world, including in medicine, mathematics and astronomy
ep.Option D: The immediate collapse of feudalism in 1099
ep.Feedback shown to students: Contact with the East expanded trade and knowledge. The Church survived and even grew stronger at first, and feudalism declined slowly for other reasons.

ep.Question: Italian cities such as Venice and Genoa benefited from the Crusades mainly because they...
ep.Option A: sent the largest armies
ep.Option B: transported and supplied Crusaders by sea and then controlled trade routes to the East
ep.Option C: were given Jerusalem to rule
ep.Feedback shown to students: Ships, supplies and loans made the Italian ports rich and gave them trading posts in the East. This wealth later helped fund the Renaissance.

ep.Question: The Crusades took place roughly between...
ep.Feedback shown to students: The First Crusade began in 1096 and the last Crusader stronghold, Acre, fell in 1291. Roughly two centuries.

ep.Question: True or false. The Crusades were caused only by religion.
ep.Option A: True
ep.Option B: False
ep.Feedback shown to students: Religion was the main stated cause, but knights also wanted land and glory, younger sons wanted inheritances they could not get at home, and merchants wanted trade. Historians look for several causes.

ep.Question: Which factor best explains how the Black Death spread from Asia to Europe in 1347?
ep.Option A: Crusader armies returning from Jerusalem
ep.Option B: Trade ships travelling along routes from the Black Sea to Italian ports such as Messina carried infected rats and fleas
ep.Option C: Pilgrims walking to Rome
ep.Feedback shown to students: The plague followed trade. Genoese ships from Caffa on the Black Sea brought it to Sicily in 1347, and it spread along trade routes and rivers from there.

ep.Question: Which TWO conditions in medieval towns helped the Black Death spread quickly?
ep.Option A: Crowded housing with poor sanitation and rubbish in the streets
ep.Option B: Advanced hospitals that gathered the sick together
ep.Option C: Very little understanding of how disease was transmitted
ep.Option D: Strict quarantine laws enforced by the king
ep.Feedback shown to students: Dirty, crowded towns suited rats and fleas, and people did not know to isolate the sick or control vermin. Quarantine came later and was patchy.

ep.Question: Why did groups of flagellants whip themselves in public during the Black Death?
ep.Option A: To cure the disease through bleeding
ep.Option B: To entertain townspeople and raise money
ep.Option C: They believed the plague was God's punishment and that suffering would earn forgiveness
ep.Option D: The Church ordered them to do it
ep.Feedback shown to students: Most people believed the plague was divine punishment. Flagellants tried to atone through pain. The Church eventually condemned them, which is why option D is wrong.

ep.Stimulus (text to paste as text stimulus:
Adapted from the Decameron by Giovanni Boccaccio, Florence, c. 1350.
"Brother abandoned brother, and very often the wife her husband. Fathers and mothers refused to see or tend their children, as if they were strangers. The sick were left with only the help of servants, who demanded high wages. So many died that bodies were stacked in pits like goods in a ship."
ep.Question: Highlight the phrase that provides evidence of an ECONOMIC effect of the plague.
ep.Feedback shown to students: Most of the source describes social breakdown. The one economic clue is that labour became scarce and expensive, which foreshadows the long-term rise in wages and the decline of serfdom.

ep.Question: Approximately what proportion of Europe's population died in the Black Death between 1347 and 1351?
ep.Option A: About 5 per cent
ep.Option B: About one tenth
ep.Option C: Between one third and one half
ep.Feedback shown to students: Estimates range from a third to a half, roughly 25 million people. This scale is why the impacts were so deep and long-lasting.

ep.Question: How did the Black Death change the position of surviving peasants?
ep.Option A: They were forced into stricter serfdom
ep.Option B: A shortage of workers allowed them to demand higher wages and better conditions, weakening the feudal system
ep.Option C: They all moved to the Holy Land
ep.Feedback shown to students: Fewer workers meant lords competed for labour. Many peasants gained wages, freedom of movement or cheaper land, and attempts to reverse this led to revolts.

ep.Question: Why did the Black Death weaken people's faith in the Catholic Church?
ep.Option A: The Church banned all religious services
ep.Option B: Prayers and processions did not stop the plague and many priests died or fled, so the Church seemed powerless
ep.Option C: The Pope converted to Islam
ep.Option D: The Church invented a cure and charged for it
ep.Feedback shown to students: The Church claimed to stand between people and God. When it could not explain or stop the plague, and clergy died like everyone else, its authority was questioned.

ep.Exam skill or knowledge tested: Cause and effect (short vs long term)
ep.Question:
Sort each impact by choosing short-term or long-term.
Mass burials in plague pits were a [short-term] impact. Rising wages for peasants were a [long-term] impact. The appearance of flagellants was a [short-term] impact. The weakening of feudalism was a [long-term] impact.
ep.Option A: Each blank offers: short-term / long-term
ep.Feedback shown to students: Short-term impacts happened during or just after the outbreak. Long-term impacts unfolded over decades as the labour shortage reshaped society.
ep.Teacher notes: Directly targets the short vs long term structure used in past short-answer questions.

ep.Question: True or false. The Black Death is considered a turning point because it caused immediate, permanent collapse of the Catholic Church.
ep.Option A: True
ep.Option B: False
ep.Feedback shown to students: The Church survived for centuries. The Black Death is a turning point because it weakened feudalism and Church authority and shifted power towards ordinary workers over the following century, not because of a sudden collapse.
ep.Teacher notes: Targets over-claiming, which appeared in the moderation samples.

ep.Question: Which statement correctly links the Crusades and the Black Death?
ep.Option A: The Crusades caused the Black Death
ep.Option B: Both increased trade and contact between Europe and the East, and the trade routes that grew after the Crusades were the same routes along which the plague travelled
ep.Option C: The Black Death ended the Crusades
ep.Feedback shown to students: The Crusades ended in 1291 and the plague arrived in 1347, so one did not directly cause the other. The link is trade. Expanded Mediterranean trade carried both goods and disease.

ep.Question: Japan is an archipelago with mountains covering about three quarters of its land. Which consequence followed most directly from this geography?
ep.Option A: Japan became a major horse-breeding nation
ep.Option B: Farming was concentrated in narrow coastal plains and valleys, and separate regions developed under local clans
ep.Option C: Japan was invaded frequently by its neighbours
ep.Feedback shown to students: Mountains divided the islands into pockets of farmland, which encouraged strong regional clans and made central control difficult. The sea also protected Japan from most invasions.

ep.Question: Which TWO ways did the sea shape early Japan?
ep.Option A: It protected Japan from invasion, including the failed Mongol attacks of 1274 and 1281
ep.Option B: It made Japan the centre of a European trading empire
ep.Option C: It provided fish and allowed coastal trade between regions
ep.Option D: It prevented any contact with China or Korea
ep.Feedback shown to students: The sea was both a shield and a source of food and trade. Contact with China and Korea did occur, bringing Buddhism and writing, so option D is wrong.

ep.Question: Why is the Genpei War (1180 to 1185) considered a turning point in Japanese history?
ep.Option A: It unified Japan under the emperor
ep.Option B: The victorious Minamoto clan set up the first shogunate, beginning almost 700 years of rule by military leaders
ep.Option C: It ended the samurai class
ep.Option D: It opened Japan to Western trade
ep.Feedback shown to students: After defeating the Taira, Minamoto Yoritomo was named shogun in 1192. From then on real power sat with military rulers, not the emperor.

ep.Question:
Complete the feudal hierarchy of Japan.
The [emperor] was the religious and ceremonial head of Japan but held little real power. The [shogun] was the military ruler who governed in his name. Powerful lords called [daimyo] controlled regions and were served by warriors called [samurai]. Below them, [peasants] farmed the land and made up most of the population.
ep.Option A: Each blank offers: emperor / shogun / daimyo / samurai / peasants / merchants
ep.Feedback shown to students: The emperor sat above the shogun in theory but below him in real power. Merchants ranked lowest among the four main classes.

ep.Question: Which statement best describes the emperor's role during the shogunate period?
ep.Option A: He commanded the samurai armies in battle
ep.Option B: He was a respected religious and ceremonial figurehead while the shogun held real political and military power
ep.Option C: He was elected by the daimyo every ten years
ep.Option D: He had been abolished by the Minamoto clan
ep.Feedback shown to students: Shoguns ruled in the emperor's name, which gave their power legitimacy. The emperor remained in Kyoto with prestige but little control. This is why restoring his power in 1868 was so symbolic.

ep.Question: What was the main difference between a daimyo and a samurai?
ep.Option A: Daimyo were religious leaders and samurai were farmers
ep.Option B: Daimyo were landholding lords who commanded armies, while samurai were the warriors who served them in return for a stipend
ep.Option C: Samurai outranked daimyo
ep.Feedback shown to students: Both belonged to the warrior class and followed bushido. The difference was rank and role. The daimyo owned the domain and the samurai served it.
ep.Teacher notes: Mirrors the compare question style. A similarity version follows.

ep.Question: Which TWO values were central to bushido?
ep.Option A: Loyalty to one's lord, even unto death
ep.Option B: Accumulating personal wealth through trade
ep.Option C: Honour, including a readiness to die rather than be disgraced
ep.Feedback shown to students: Bushido emphasised loyalty, honour, courage, discipline and frugality. Trade was considered beneath a samurai and equality contradicted the hierarchy.

ep.Question: A samurai whose lord was killed through his failure might commit seppuku. What does this reveal about bushido?
ep.Option A: That samurai feared punishment from the emperor
ep.Option B: That honour and loyalty were valued above the samurai's own life
ep.Option C: That samurai were poorly trained
ep.Option D: That seppuku was a form of medical treatment
ep.Feedback shown to students: Seppuku restored honour after failure or disgrace. It shows how completely bushido tied a samurai's identity to loyalty and honour.

ep.Question: What is the term for a samurai who has no master or lord? (one word)
ep.Feedback shown to students: Ronin means wave man, someone adrift. Numbers grew after Sekigahara when defeated daimyo lost their domains and their samurai lost their positions.
ep.Teacher notes: EP Textbox. Accept ronin and Ronin.

ep.Exam skill or knowledge tested: Daimyo and the fall of the Ashikaga
ep.Question: How did the daimyo contribute to the collapse of the Ashikaga shogunate in the 15th and 16th centuries?
ep.Option A: They supported the shogun loyally
ep.Option B: They built independent armies and fought each other for land, so the shogun lost control and Japan fell into the Sengoku, or Warring States, period
ep.Option C: They invited Western powers to rule Japan
ep.Feedback shown to students: A weak shogun could not restrain powerful regional lords. The Onin War (1467 to 1477) triggered a century of civil war that only ended with Sekigahara in 1600.

ep.Question: What did Tokugawa Ieyasu do after winning the Battle of Sekigahara in 1600?
ep.Option A: He restored the emperor to full power
ep.Option B: He became shogun in 1603 and set up a government at Edo that brought over 250 years of peace
ep.Option C: He opened Japan to American trade
ep.Feedback shown to students: Ieyasu used victory to found the Tokugawa shogunate. Edo, today's Tokyo, became the political centre of Japan.

ep.Question: The policy of sankin kotai required daimyo to spend alternate years in Edo and leave their families there when they returned home. What was its main purpose?
ep.Option A: To educate the daimyo's children
ep.Option B: To keep daimyo under the shogun's watch, drain their wealth through travel and hold their families as hostages against rebellion
ep.Option C: To improve Japan's roads
ep.Feedback shown to students: Sankin kotai was about control. It cost daimyo heavily, kept them visible and made rebellion risky. Better roads and a booming Edo were side effects, not the purpose.

ep.Question: What is an edict?
ep.Option A: A type of samurai sword
ep.Option B: An official order issued by the shogun or another authority that people were required to obey
ep.Option C: A Buddhist prayer
ep.Feedback shown to students: The Tokugawa governed through edicts, such as the Laws for Military Houses controlling daimyo and the sakoku edicts restricting foreign contact.

ep.Stimulus (text to paste as text stimulus:
Adapted from the Laws for the Military Houses (Buke Shohatto), issued by the Tokugawa shogunate, 1615.
"Daimyo must not repair their castles without permission, and new construction is strictly forbidden. Daimyo must report at once any plot or disturbance in a neighbouring domain. Marriages between daimyo families must not be arranged privately. The lords must live simply and avoid luxury."
ep.Question: Highlight the rule that was designed to stop daimyo forming alliances against the shogun.
ep.Correct answer: Marriages between daimyo families must not be arranged privately
ep.Feedback shown to students: Marriage created alliances between clans. Controlling it stopped rival daimyo from uniting. The castle rule limited military strength and the reporting rule turned daimyo into informers on each other.

ep.Question: Which TWO statements about sakoku are correct?
ep.Option A: Japanese people were forbidden to leave Japan, and those overseas could not return
ep.Option B: All foreign trade was completely banned
ep.Option C: Limited trade continued with the Dutch and Chinese at Nagasaki
ep.Option D: Sakoku was introduced by the Meiji government
ep.Feedback shown to students: Sakoku was near-isolation, not total isolation. A controlled window at Nagasaki let the shogunate monitor foreign ideas and goods. It was a Tokugawa policy, ended under pressure in the 1850s.

ep.Question: Why did the Tokugawa shoguns adopt sakoku in the 1630s?
ep.Option A: Japan had run out of goods to trade
ep.Option B: They feared that Christianity and foreign influence would undermine their control and that daimyo might gain wealth and weapons through foreign trade
ep.Option C: The emperor demanded it
ep.Option D: To prepare for an invasion of China
ep.Feedback shown to students: The Shimabara Rebellion of 1637 to 1638 confirmed the shoguns' fear of Christianity as a rival loyalty. Restricting trade also stopped daimyo arming themselves through foreign contacts.

ep.Question: Under the Tokugawa four-class system, merchants ranked below farmers and artisans even though many merchants became wealthy. What does this show about the system?
ep.Option A: That wealth was the basis of status
ep.Option B: That status was based on perceived usefulness to society, and merchants were seen as profiting from others' work
ep.Option C: That merchants were foreigners
ep.Option D: That farmers were the richest class
ep.Feedback shown to students: The gap between official rank and real wealth grew during the long peace and became a source of tension, as impoverished samurai borrowed from the merchants they officially outranked.

ep.Question: Which development in Edo-period cities shows that the long peace changed Japanese society?
ep.Option A: Constant civil war between daimyo
ep.Option B: A flourishing urban culture including kabuki theatre, woodblock prints and pleasure districts, supported by a growing merchant class
ep.Option C: The abolition of the samurai
ep.Feedback shown to students: Peace let cities grow and merchants prosper, which paid for a lively popular culture. Samurai, meanwhile, became administrators rather than fighters.

ep.Question:
Decide whether each Tokugawa policy mainly produced continuity or change.
Banning private wars between daimyo preserved the shogun's authority, so it created political [continuity]. The same ban turned samurai into officials rather than fighters, which was a social [change]. Sankin kotai kept the daimyo loyal, which was [continuity], but the travelling and spending it required made Edo into a huge commercial city, which was economic [change].
ep.Option A: Each blank offers: continuity / change
ep.Feedback shown to students: One policy can produce both. Ask what stayed the same (who held power) and what shifted (how people lived and earned a living).
ep.Teacher notes: Directly reflects the 2025 exam's continuity and change framing of Tokugawa restrictions.

ep.Question: Which problem had weakened the Tokugawa shogunate from within before Perry arrived in 1853?
ep.Option A: Too many foreign wars
ep.Option B: Samurai stipends paid in rice lost value while merchants grew rich, and peasants suffered famines and rising taxes, causing unrest
ep.Option C: The emperor commanded the army
ep.Feedback shown to students: Historians argue Perry was the trigger, not the only cause. Financial strain on samurai, peasant revolts and a rigid class system made the shogunate vulnerable to the shock of Western pressure.
ep.Teacher notes: Sets up the contestability of the Perry question in the extended response.

ep.Question: What did Commodore Matthew Perry demand when he arrived in Edo Bay in 1853?
ep.Option A: That Japan convert to Christianity
ep.Option B: That Japan open its ports to American ships for trade, supplies and the protection of shipwrecked sailors
ep.Option C: That the emperor abdicate
ep.Option D: That Japan join a war against China
ep.Feedback shown to students: Perry carried a letter from the US President and returned in 1854 with more warships. The Treaty of Kanagawa opened two ports and ended more than 200 years of sakoku.

ep.Question: Why did the shogunate's response to Perry weaken its authority?
ep.Option A: The shogun defeated Perry but lost many ships
ep.Option B: The shogunate gave in to foreign demands, which showed it could not fulfil its basic duty of protecting Japan and angered many daimyo and samurai
ep.Option C: The shogun travelled to America
ep.Feedback shown to students: The shogun's title literally meant barbarian-subduing general. Signing unequal treaties under threat destroyed the shogunate's claim to rule.

ep.Question: In the 1860s the slogan 'Revere the emperor, expel the barbarians' was popular among some samurai. Which perspective does this reveal?
ep.Option A: Support for the shogun's treaties
ep.Option B: Anger at foreign intrusion combined with the belief that loyalty should return to the emperor rather than a failed shogun
ep.Option C: A desire to become American citizens
ep.Feedback shown to students: Many lower-ranking samurai, especially in Satsuma and Choshu, saw the emperor as the symbol of a united Japan that could resist the West. Ironically, once in power they embraced Western methods.

ep.Question: What happened in 1868?
ep.Option A: Perry arrived in Japan
ep.Option B: The last Tokugawa shogun gave up power and rule was restored to the emperor, who took the name Meiji
ep.Option C: Japan defeated Russia
ep.Feedback shown to students: 1868 marks the Meiji Restoration. Perry came in 1853, Sekigahara was 1600 and the war with Russia was 1904 to 1905.

ep.Question: Which TWO were reforms introduced during the Meiji period?
ep.Option A: A national conscript army replacing samurai armies, introduced in 1873
ep.Option B: The reintroduction of sakoku
ep.Option C: Compulsory education for all children
ep.Feedback shown to students: The Meiji government built a modern army, schools, railways, factories and a constitution (1889). Sakoku was abandoned, not restored, and the emperor was at the centre of the new state.

ep.Question: What happened to the samurai class after the Meiji Restoration?
ep.Option A: They became the new ruling class
ep.Option B: Their privileges were abolished, including the right to carry swords and receive stipends, and the class was officially ended by the 1870s
ep.Option C: They were all sent overseas
ep.Feedback shown to students: A modern conscript army made a hereditary warrior class unnecessary. Some samurai joined government or business, while others rebelled, most famously in the Satsuma Rebellion of 1877.

ep.Question:
Choose continuity or change for each statement about Japan after 1868.
The emperor remained the symbolic head of the nation, which is [continuity]. The feudal domains were replaced by prefectures run by the central government, which is [change]. Japan continued to be ruled by a small elite rather than by the people, which is [continuity]. Western dress, railways and factories transformed daily life in cities, which is [change].
ep.Option A: Each blank offers: continuity / change
ep.Feedback shown to students: The Restoration changed how Japan was governed and how people lived, but the emperor and elite rule continued. Strong answers notice both.

ep.Question: Japan adopted Western technology, military methods and a constitution but kept the emperor, Shinto and many traditions. Which statement best describes this?
ep.Option A: Japan became a Western country
ep.Option B: Japan modernised selectively, taking what would make it strong enough to resist the West while keeping its own identity
ep.Option C: Japan rejected all change
ep.Option D: Japan was colonised by the United States
ep.Feedback shown to students: The Meiji slogan was rich country, strong army. Modernisation was a strategy for independence. Westernisation describes the cultural borrowing that came with it, and the two are not the same thing.
ep.Teacher notes: The moderation notes flagged confusion between modernisation and westernisation.

ep.Question: Which outcome best shows the significance of the Meiji Restoration?
ep.Option A: Japan remained isolated for another century
ep.Option B: Within 40 years Japan had become an industrial and military power able to defeat Russia in 1905, the first modern victory of an Asian nation over a European one
ep.Option C: Japan was divided into two countries
ep.Feedback shown to students: Significance is judged by scale and consequence. A feudal society became a world power within one lifetime, which reshaped Asia.

ep.Question: Which statement correctly connects feudal Japan, the Tokugawa shogunate and the Meiji Restoration?
ep.Option A: The Meiji Restoration created the samurai
ep.Option B: The Tokugawa used the feudal hierarchy and strict control to keep peace for 250 years, but the same rigidity left Japan unable to respond to Western pressure, and the Meiji government dismantled the feudal system to modernise
ep.Option C: The three periods had nothing to do with each other
ep.Option D: The Tokugawa were overthrown by the Crusaders
ep.Feedback shown to students: Each period set up the next. Feudal loyalty gave the Tokugawa a system to control. Tokugawa stability bred the weaknesses Perry exposed. The Meiji leaders replaced feudalism with a modern state.
ep.Teacher notes: This is the synthesis the essay booklet is built around.

ep.Question: Write ONE TEEAL paragraph in response to the following. Analyse the significance of the Crusades for medieval Europe. Your paragraph should state a clear argument, include at least two specific pieces of historical evidence, explain how the evidence supports your argument and link back to the question.
ep.Feedback shown to students: Strong responses argue for a specific significance (trade, Church power, knowledge, Italian cities) rather than listing effects, and explain why that change mattered over the long term.
ep.Teacher notes: Marking guide suggestion out of 8. Analysis 3, knowledge 2, structure 1, writing 2, to match the exam rubric.

ep.Question: Explain why the Black Death weakened the feudal system. Write one paragraph of 6 to 8 sentences. Include a specific cause, at least one piece of evidence and a clear explanation of the link between the plague and the decline of feudalism.
ep.Feedback shown to students: Look for the chain. Population loss, labour shortage, peasants demanding wages or moving, lords unable to enforce old obligations, revolts when they tried.
ep.Teacher notes: Short-answer style practice for the 3 to 4 mark explain questions.

ep.Question: Write ONE TEEAL paragraph in response to the following. Evaluate how the Catholic Church maintained its influence over medieval society. Choose the type of power you think mattered most (political, social, economic or cultural), support it with at least two specific examples and explain why it was more important than the others.
ep.Feedback shown to students: Strong responses pick one form of power and argue for it, rather than listing all four. Credit a judgement about why that form underpinned the rest, for example that spiritual authority made the tithe and excommunication possible.
ep.Teacher notes: Covers the evaluate-an-institution skill from the exam overview without reusing the 2024 essay prompt.

ep.Question: Some historians argue that Commodore Perry's arrival caused the fall of the Tokugawa shogunate. Others argue the shogunate was already failing. Write ONE TEEAL paragraph that takes a position and supports it with evidence from both internal problems and external pressure.
ep.Feedback shown to students: The best responses weigh both and reach a judgement, for example that Perry was the trigger that exposed existing weaknesses.
ep.Teacher notes: Prepares the Perry essay without reusing the exam wording.

ep.Question: To what extent did the Meiji Restoration transform Japan? Write ONE TEEAL paragraph. Identify at least two major changes and one important continuity, and reach a judgement about how far Japan was transformed.
ep.Feedback shown to students: Reward specific reforms (conscription 1873, compulsory education, prefectures, 1889 constitution, railways) and a recognised continuity (emperor, elite rule, Shinto). The judgement matters more than the list.

soc_exam.q: What was the main purpose of feudalism in medieval Europe?
opts: To organise society through land, loyalty and service
To spread Christianity to other countries
soc_exam.expl: Feudalism was a system of land for service. Everything else, from castles to knights, grew out of that exchange.

soc_exam.q: Which statement BEST describes the relationship between a lord and a vassal?
opts: The vassal paid the lord a tithe
The lord granted land to the vassal in return for loyalty and military service
The vassal gave land to the lord in return for protection
The lord and vassal were equals who shared land
soc_exam.expl: The lord gave the fief, the vassal gave loyalty and service. Vassals could themselves be lords to knights below them.

soc_exam.q: What was the role of peasants in the feudal system?
opts: They fought in the king's army as knights
They worked the land and produced the food that supported everyone above them
They collected taxes for the king
soc_exam.expl: Peasants were the largest group and the base of the pyramid. Without their labour the rest of the hierarchy could not exist.

soc_exam.q: Select ALL that were expectations of a knight under the code of chivalry.
soc_exam.expl: Chivalry combined loyalty, courage, protection of the weak and service to the Church. Castles and tournaments were part of knightly life but not rules of the code.

soc_exam.q: Why were punishments in medieval Europe usually carried out in public?
opts: To shame the offender and warn others against committing the same crime
To let the crowd decide if the punishment was fair
To show the wealth of the offender
To allow the accused to prove innocence
soc_exam.expl: With no police force, public punishment was the main deterrent.

soc_exam.q: What was the role of a castle in medieval Europe beyond defence?
opts: It was a place for peasants to live
It was a symbol of the lord's power and the centre for collecting taxes and giving justice
It was a market for merchants
soc_exam.expl: A castle announced who controlled the land. Government, justice and the lord's wealth were all inside it.

soc_exam.q: Select ALL the ways the Catholic Church influenced everyday life in medieval Europe.
opts: It collected a tithe of one tenth of what people produced
It marked every stage of life from baptism to burial
It controlled education and preserved books through monasteries
soc_exam.expl: The Church touched daily life through money, ritual and learning. It crowned kings but did not elect them.

soc_exam.q: How did the Church keep its power over people who could not read?
opts: Through paintings of heaven and hell, the threat of excommunication and control of the sacraments
By paying people to attend church
soc_exam.expl: Doom paintings, sermons and the sacraments made Church teaching visible. Fear of hell did the rest.

soc_exam.q: What was the main aim of the First Crusade?
opts: To capture Jerusalem and the Holy Land from Muslim rule
soc_exam.expl: Pope Urban II called for the recovery of Jerusalem in 1095. Trade and land were motives for some Crusaders but not the stated aim.

soc_exam.q: Which consequence of the Crusades is shown by this source? 'People from different cultures now speak one another's languages. Merchants frequently arrive by sea, bringing goods from many different places.'
opts: The end of the Catholic Church
Increased trade and cultural exchange between Europe and the East
The spread of the Black Death
soc_exam.expl: The source describes contact and trade. Reading the evidence in the source, not just recalling facts, is what the exam rewards.

soc_exam.q: Which factor contributed MOST to the spread of the Black Death through Europe?
opts: Trade routes and ships carrying infected rats and fleas between ports
Castles being built too close together
soc_exam.expl: The plague followed trade from the Black Sea to Messina in 1347 and then along roads and rivers.

soc_exam.q: Which was a LONG-TERM consequence of the Black Death?
opts: Flagellants whipping themselves in the streets
A labour shortage that gave surviving peasants bargaining power and weakened feudalism
soc_exam.expl: The first three happened during the outbreak. The labour shortage reshaped society for a century.

soc_exam.q: A source is captioned 'Illuminated manuscript produced in Italy, c. 1290'. In which century was it created and what type of source is it?
soc_exam.expl: 1290 is in the 1200s, the 13th century. A manuscript made at the time is a primary source.

soc_exam.q: Identify one crime committed in medieval Europe and describe one likely punishment for it.
soc_exam.expl: Model answer. Theft, punished by a fine, time in the stocks, or for repeat offenders cutting off a hand. Or treason, punished by execution and loss of property.

soc_exam.q: Explain one way the Black Death weakened the power of the Catholic Church.
soc_exam.expl: Model answer. Prayers and processions did not stop the plague and many priests died or fled, so people began to doubt that the Church could protect them or explain God's will.

soc_exam.q: How did Japan's geography influence its early development?
opts: Flat plains made it easy to unite the country
Mountains and islands separated regions, so strong local clans developed and farming was limited to coastal plains and valleys
Japan was easily invaded by China
soc_exam.expl: Geography made central control hard and local loyalty strong, which is the root of Japanese feudalism.

soc_exam.q: Why is the Genpei War (1180 to 1185) a turning point in Japanese history?
opts: The Minamoto victory led to the first shogunate, beginning almost 700 years of rule by military leaders
Japan was conquered by the Mongols
soc_exam.expl: Minamoto Yoritomo became shogun in 1192. Real power moved from the emperor to the shogun.

soc_exam.q: Who held the greatest political and military power in shogunate Japan?
soc_exam.expl: The shogun ruled in the emperor's name. The emperor kept prestige but little power.

soc_exam.q: Compare the daimyo and the samurai. Which statement is correct?
opts: Both belonged to the warrior class and followed bushido, but daimyo controlled domains while samurai served them
Daimyo were peasants who became warriors
soc_exam.expl: Similarity, warrior class and bushido. Difference, rank and role. The exam asks for both.

soc_exam.q: Select ALL that were values of the bushido code.
soc_exam.expl: Bushido was about loyalty, honour and discipline. Trade was beneath a samurai and equality contradicted the hierarchy.

soc_exam.q: Why did the Tokugawa shogunate rank farmers above merchants?
opts: Farmers produced food, which was seen as essential, while merchants were seen as profiting from others' work
soc_exam.expl: Status was based on usefulness to society, not wealth. Over time rich merchants and poor samurai made this a source of tension.

soc_exam.q: What was the significance of Tokugawa Ieyasu?
opts: He restored the emperor to power in 1868
After winning the Battle of Sekigahara in 1600 he became shogun and founded a dynasty that ruled for over 250 years
He opened Japan to American trade
soc_exam.expl: Ieyasu ended a century of civil war and built the system of control that kept Japan at peace until the 1860s.

soc_exam.q: Select ALL the purposes of sankin kotai.
opts: To keep daimyo under the shogun's observation in Edo
To drain daimyo wealth through the cost of travel and two households
To hold daimyo families in Edo as hostages against rebellion
soc_exam.expl: Observation, expense and hostages. The policy was about preventing rebellion.

soc_exam.q: Define the term edict. Which option is correct?
opts: An official order from the shogun or another authority that people were required to obey
soc_exam.expl: Examples include the Laws for Military Houses controlling daimyo, the sakoku edicts and the ban on Christianity.

soc_exam.q: Why did the Tokugawa shoguns ban Christianity?
opts: It created loyalty to a foreign religion and foreign powers that could challenge the shogun's authority
soc_exam.expl: Converted daimyo had divided loyalties and missionaries were linked to European influence. The Shimabara Rebellion confirmed the shoguns' fears.

soc_exam.q: Which statement about sakoku is FALSE?
opts: Japanese people were forbidden to leave Japan
Limited trade continued with the Dutch and Chinese at Nagasaki
All contact with the outside world was completely cut off
soc_exam.expl: Sakoku was near-isolation, not total isolation. A controlled window at Nagasaki stayed open.

soc_exam.q: Which internal problem weakened the Tokugawa shogunate BEFORE Commodore Perry arrived in 1853?
opts: Samurai fell into poverty and debt during the long peace while merchants grew rich
Japan lost a war to China
Daimyo were allowed to build castles freely
soc_exam.expl: Historians argue Perry was the trigger that exposed existing weaknesses, including poor samurai, peasant unrest and a rigid class system.

soc_exam.q: What were the main consequences of the Meiji Restoration of 1868?
opts: Power returned to the emperor, the feudal system was abolished and Japan rapidly modernised its army, industry and education
Japan was colonised by the United States
soc_exam.expl: Within 40 years Japan went from a feudal society to an industrial and military power.

soc_exam.q: Explain one reason Japan adopted the policy of sakoku.
soc_exam.expl: Model answer. The shoguns feared that Christianity and foreign trade would give daimyo outside allies, wealth and weapons that could be used against the shogunate, so they restricted contact to keep control.

soc_exam.q: Explain how Commodore Perry's arrival in 1853 contributed to the fall of the Tokugawa shogunate.
soc_exam.expl: Model answer. Perry's warships forced the shogun to sign unequal treaties and open ports. This showed the shogunate could not protect Japan, so daimyo and samurai lost faith in it and rallied to the emperor, leading to its collapse in 1868.

soc_warm.q: Which pair correctly matches a European feudal role with its closest Japanese equivalent?
soc_warm.expl: Nobles and daimyo were both landholding lords who owed loyalty to a higher ruler and commanded their own warriors. The shogun was closer to a king in real power, and the emperor had little.

soc_warm.q: In both medieval Europe and shogunate Japan, land was granted in return for...
soc_warm.expl: Land for service is the core of feudalism in both societies.

soc_warm.q: Which event happened FIRST?
opts: Minamoto Yoritomo becomes the first shogun
soc_warm.expl: First Crusade 1096, Yoritomo 1192, Black Death 1347, Sekigahara 1600.

soc_warm.q: A source is captioned 'Woodblock print, Edo, 1830'. Which statement about its origin is correct?
opts: It was made in the 18th century under the Tokugawa
It was made in the 19th century under the Tokugawa
It was made in the 19th century after the Meiji Restoration
It was made in the 17th century during sakoku
soc_warm.expl: 1830 is the 19th century. The Tokugawa ruled until 1868 and Edo was their capital.

soc_warm.q: Why did a medieval serf find it so hard to improve his position in society?
opts: He was legally bound to the lord's land and owed labour he could not refuse
He was not allowed to attend church
He was required to become a knight
He had to pay the Pope directly
soc_warm.expl: Serfs were tied to the manor. Freedom of movement, not wealth, was the key restriction.

soc_warm.q: Select ALL that were reasons people joined the First Crusade.
opts: The promise of forgiveness of sins
The chance to gain land and wealth
To free Jerusalem from Muslim rule
soc_warm.expl: Religion, land and the Holy Land all motivated Crusaders. The Black Death came 250 years later and Japan was unknown to Europeans.

soc_warm.q: Which consequence of the Crusades had the longest-lasting effect on Europe?
opts: Jerusalem stayed in Christian hands permanently
Trade and contact with the East expanded, bringing goods, knowledge and wealth to Italian cities
All European kings lost their power
soc_warm.expl: The Crusader states were lost by 1291 but the trade links remained and helped fund the Renaissance.

soc_warm.q: The Black Death arrived in Europe in 1347 through...
opts: Crusader knights returning from the Holy Land
trade ships docking at Sicilian and Italian ports
Mongol armies invading from the east
soc_warm.expl: The plague followed trade routes from the Black Sea to Messina and then inland.

soc_warm.q: What did flagellants believe?
opts: That the plague was God's punishment and self-inflicted pain would earn forgiveness
That the Pope had caused the plague
That the plague could be cured with herbs
soc_warm.expl: Most medieval people saw the plague as divine punishment. Flagellants took that belief to an extreme.

soc_warm.q: Which was a LONG-TERM effect of the Black Death?
opts: Peasants demanding higher wages as labour became scarce
Church services cancelled during the outbreak
soc_warm.expl: The other three happened during the outbreak. The labour shortage reshaped society over decades.

soc_warm.q: How did the Black Death affect the Catholic Church?
opts: It made the Church more powerful than ever
Faith was shaken because prayer did not stop the plague and many clergy died or fled
The Church gained control of all medicine
soc_warm.expl: The Church's authority rested on explaining the world. Its failure to stop the plague raised doubts that grew over the following century.

soc_warm.q: Japan's mountainous islands led to...
opts: a single united kingdom from earliest times
strong regional clans and farming concentrated on narrow coastal plains
frequent invasion by Korea and China
soc_warm.expl: Mountains divided the land into regions, which made strong local clans and weak central control likely.

soc_warm.q: Who held real political power in Japan after 1192?
soc_warm.expl: From Yoritomo onwards the shogun governed in the emperor's name while the emperor remained a figurehead in Kyoto.

soc_warm.q: Which statement about samurai and daimyo is a SIMILARITY?
opts: Both belonged to the warrior class and followed bushido
soc_warm.expl: The difference was rank. Daimyo were lords, samurai served them. The code and class were shared.

soc_warm.q: A samurai chooses death over surrender after his lord is defeated. This BEST shows which bushido value?
soc_warm.expl: Loyalty to the lord and personal honour outranked survival in bushido.

soc_warm.q: Tokugawa Ieyasu's victory at Sekigahara in 1600 was significant because it...
opts: allowed him to become shogun and begin 250 years of peace under his family
soc_warm.expl: Significance comes from the consequence. One battle set up two and a half centuries of Tokugawa rule.

soc_warm.q: Select ALL the ways sankin kotai helped the shogun control the daimyo.
opts: It kept daimyo under observation in Edo
It drained daimyo wealth through constant travel
It held daimyo families in Edo as hostages
It allowed daimyo to trade with Europe
soc_warm.expl: Observation, expense and hostages. The policy was about control, not reward.

soc_warm.q: Which statement about sakoku is FALSE?
opts: Japanese people could not leave Japan
All contact with the outside world was cut off
The Dutch and Chinese could trade at Nagasaki
soc_warm.expl: Sakoku was near-isolation. A controlled trade window at Nagasaki stayed open for over 200 years.

soc_warm.q: Under the Tokugawa, merchants grew rich but ranked at the bottom of the four classes. What problem did this cause over time?
opts: Samurai with fixed rice stipends fell into debt to the merchants they officially outranked, creating resentment
soc_warm.expl: The gap between official rank and real wealth was one of the internal weaknesses of the shogunate before Perry arrived.

soc_warm.q: Commodore Perry arrived in Japan in 1853 with...
opts: warships and a demand that Japan open its ports to trade
soc_warm.expl: Perry's steam warships demonstrated Western power. Japan could not refuse and signed the Treaty of Kanagawa in 1854.

soc_warm.q: Why did many samurai turn against the shogun after 1854?
opts: The shogun had given in to foreign demands and seemed unable to protect Japan
The shogun moved the capital to Kyoto
soc_warm.expl: Protecting Japan from outsiders was the shogun's whole purpose. Signing unequal treaties destroyed his authority.

soc_warm.q: Select ALL that were Meiji reforms.
soc_warm.expl: The Meiji leaders modernised Japan to resist the West. Isolation ended and the emperor became the symbol of the new nation.

soc_warm.q: Japan copied Western technology and government but kept the emperor and Shinto. The best word for this is...
soc_warm.expl: Japan modernised on its own terms. Westernisation describes the cultural borrowing, modernisation describes the goal.

soc_warm.q: In one sentence, explain why historians call the Battle of Hastings OR the Genpei War a turning point.
soc_warm.expl: Model answer. The Genpei War ended with Yoritomo becoming shogun in 1192, shifting real power from the emperor to military rulers for the next 700 years. Or, Hastings in 1066 brought Norman rule and the feudal system to England.

soc_warm.q: Name one short-term and one long-term impact of the Black Death.
soc_warm.expl: Model answer. Short-term, mass deaths and plague pits or flagellants. Long-term, labour shortages raised wages and weakened feudalism, and faith in the Church declined.

soc_warm.q: Give one piece of evidence that the Tokugawa shogunate was already weakening BEFORE Perry arrived.
soc_warm.expl: Model answer. Samurai in debt to merchants, peasant uprisings and famines, or daimyo in the south-west (Satsuma, Choshu) resenting Tokugawa control.

soc_me.q: In the feudal system, a lord granted land to a vassal in return for...
soc_me.expl: Land for service is the core of feudalism. The land was the fief, the person receiving it was the vassal.

soc_me.q: Put the feudal hierarchy in order from the top. Which option is correct?
soc_me.expl: Land flowed down from the monarch to nobles to knights. Peasants worked the land at the bottom.

soc_me.q: Why did a medieval serf find it so hard to improve his position in society?
opts: He was legally bound to the lord's land and owed labour he could not refuse
He was not allowed to attend church
He was required to become a knight
He had to pay the Pope directly
soc_me.expl: Serfs were tied to the manor. Freedom of movement, not wealth, was the key restriction.

soc_me.q: How did feudalism help a king control a large kingdom without a police force or a paid army?
opts: Every peasant swore an oath to the king personally
Nobles who held land from the king had to supply knights and keep order in their own regions
soc_me.expl: The king could not be everywhere. Granting land made nobles responsible for defence and order in return for their oath.

soc_me.q: Select ALL that were expectations of a knight under the code of chivalry.
opts: Protect the weak and the Church
soc_me.expl: Chivalry demanded loyalty, courage, protection of the weak and service to the Church. It did not extend equality to peasants.

soc_me.q: Why were medieval punishments usually carried out in public?
opts: To shame the offender and deter others, since there was no police force
soc_me.expl: With no police, fear of public punishment was the main way to keep order.

soc_me.q: A person accused of a crime carries a red-hot iron and the wound is checked three days later. This is...
soc_me.expl: Trial by ordeal asked God to reveal guilt through the outcome. It was replaced by juries after 1215.

soc_me.q: Which crime was punished most severely in medieval Europe?
soc_me.expl: Treason attacked the king himself and was punished by death and loss of all property.

soc_me.q: Besides defence, why were castles important to a lord's power?
opts: They stored all the kingdom's grain
They were a visible symbol of authority and the centre for collecting taxes and giving justice
soc_me.expl: A castle told everyone who ruled the region. The lord's court, treasury and soldiers were inside it.

soc_me.q: How did castle design change between 1066 and 1300?
opts: Stone castles were replaced by wooden ones
Wooden motte-and-bailey castles were replaced by stone keeps and then concentric stone castles
soc_me.expl: Stone resisted fire and siege engines. The purpose stayed the same while the form changed, which is continuity and change.

soc_me.q: Select ALL the ways the Catholic Church was part of an ordinary villager's everyday life.
opts: Baptism, marriage and burial happened in the church
Villagers paid a tithe of one tenth of their produce
The year was organised around holy days and festivals
soc_me.expl: The Church set the calendar, marked every life event and took a share of every harvest.

soc_me.q: What was the most important source of the Church's power in medieval Europe?
opts: It controlled the path to heaven in a society where almost everyone feared hell
The Pope was King of England
soc_me.expl: Spiritual power came first. Land, wealth and political influence were built on it.

soc_me.q: How could the Pope put pressure on a king who defied him?
opts: Send the Crusaders to attack him
Excommunicate him, cutting him off from the Church and giving his subjects a reason to disobey
soc_me.expl: Excommunication was a political weapon. Nobles feared for their own souls if they stayed loyal to an excommunicated king.

soc_me.q: Which of these shows the Church's CULTURAL power rather than political or economic power?
opts: Owning about one third of the land in Europe
Monks copying books and running schools
soc_me.expl: Cultural power is about learning, ideas and art. The other options are economic or political.

soc_me.q: Select ALL that were reasons people joined the First Crusade.
opts: The promise of forgiveness of sins
The chance to gain land and wealth
To free Jerusalem from Muslim rule
soc_me.expl: Religion, land and the Holy Land all motivated Crusaders. The Black Death came 250 years later.

soc_me.q: How would a Muslim living in Jerusalem in 1099 most likely have seen the Crusaders?
soc_me.expl: Perspectives depend on position. To Crusaders it was liberation. To the city's inhabitants, many of whom were killed, it was conquest.

soc_me.q: Which consequence of the Crusades had the longest-lasting effect on Europe?
opts: Jerusalem stayed in Christian hands permanently
Trade and contact with the East expanded, bringing goods, knowledge and wealth to Italian cities
All European kings lost their power
soc_me.expl: The Crusader states were lost by 1291, but the trade links remained and helped fund the Renaissance.

soc_me.q: The Crusades took place roughly between...
soc_me.expl: The First Crusade began in 1096 and the last Crusader stronghold fell in 1291.

soc_me.q: The Black Death arrived in Europe in 1347 through...
opts: Crusader knights returning from the Holy Land
trade ships docking at Sicilian and Italian ports
Mongol armies invading from the east
soc_me.expl: The plague followed trade routes from the Black Sea to Messina and then inland.

soc_me.q: What did flagellants believe?
opts: That the plague was God's punishment and self-inflicted pain would earn forgiveness
That the Pope had caused the plague
That the plague could be cured with herbs
soc_me.expl: Most medieval people saw the plague as divine punishment. Flagellants took that belief to an extreme.

soc_me.q: Which was a LONG-TERM effect of the Black Death?
opts: Peasants demanding higher wages as labour became scarce
Church services cancelled during the outbreak
soc_me.expl: The other three happened during the outbreak. The labour shortage reshaped society over decades.

soc_me.q: How did the Black Death affect the Catholic Church?
opts: It made the Church more powerful than ever
Faith was shaken because prayer did not stop the plague and many clergy died or fled
The Church gained control of all medicine
soc_me.expl: The Church claimed to explain the world. Its failure to stop the plague raised doubts that grew over the following century.

soc_me.q: A source is captioned 'Illuminated manuscript, Paris, c. 1250'. Which statement about its origin is correct?
opts: It was made in the 12th century
It was made in the 13th century
It was made in the 14th century
It was made after the Black Death
soc_me.expl: 1250 is in the 1200s, which is the 13th century. The Black Death came a century later.

soc_me.q: Which event happened FIRST?
opts: The fall of Acre ends the Crusades
soc_me.expl: Hastings 1066, First Crusade 1096, fall of Acre 1291, Black Death 1347.

soc_me.q: In one sentence, explain why the Black Death is considered a turning point in history.
soc_me.expl: Model answer. It killed a third to a half of Europe's population, which weakened feudalism and the Church's authority and shifted power towards ordinary workers over the following century.

soc_me.q: Name one short-term and one long-term impact of the Black Death.
soc_me.expl: Model answer. Short-term, mass deaths and plague pits or flagellants. Long-term, labour shortages raised wages and weakened feudalism, and faith in the Church declined.

soc_me.q: Give one way the Crusades strengthened the Catholic Church and one way the Black Death weakened it.
soc_me.expl: Model answer. The Crusades showed the Pope could unite kings and knights behind one cause and brought the Church land and wealth. The Black Death showed the Church could not stop or explain the plague, and many clergy died or fled.

terms.def: An area that contains a chain or group of islands scattered in lakes, rivers or the ocean.
The Japanese term for the shogunate government, translating to 'tent government'.
The code of behaviour of the samurai that required honour, loyalty (even to death), good living, thrift and martial arts skill.
Church law, especially in the Catholic Church, laid down by papal pronouncements.
The link between what causes an action or motivates someone to act in a certain way, and the outcome of that action.
The religion based on the person and teachings of Jesus Christ.
People ordained for religious duties, especially in the Christian church.
The idea that an interpretation or hypothesis may be challenged or left open to debate because of a lack of evidence or a different perspective.
The recognition that while many things change over time, some quite drastically, other things continue, even if in modified forms.
A series of wars fought by Christians and Muslims between 1096 and 1291 CE over control of the Holy Land.
A Japanese lord, vassal to the shogun.
An official order issued by the shogun or another authority in Japan that people were expected to obey.
The ability to understand what happened in the past by imagining how people living at the time thought, felt and experienced events, without judging them by today's values.
A sovereign ruler of great power and rank. Under the shogunate the emperor was a ceremonial and religious figurehead while governing power was in the hands of the shogun.
The information or clues discovered by asking specific questions about a historical source.
A religious punishment that cut someone off from the church community and its sacraments, such as communion, confession and entry to heaven.
A set of legal and military customs that organised the society of medieval Europe. A lord gave a fief to a vassal in exchange for loyalty and support.
Land given by a lord to a vassal in medieval Europe in return for loyalty and service.
A group of radical Christians during the Black Death who whipped themselves to gain God's forgiveness for their sins.
Doing or saying something regarded by the medieval Catholic Church as being in serious conflict with its teachings.
A way of organising people so that the most important is at the top, with others ranked underneath in decreasing order of importance. Social hierarchy arranges people according to power and wealth.
The territory in today's Middle East now mostly made up of Israel and Palestine.
A medieval warrior of Europe who pledged his services to a lord, sometimes to a king, in exchange for a fief.
A king or queen who administered the country, planned or fought wars and owned the land on which they ruled. The monarch sat at the top of the social hierarchy.
Wealthy subjects who lived on land granted to them (fiefs) in large manor houses. They were below the monarch on the social hierarchy.
A person rejected by Japanese society because their occupation conflicted with religious beliefs, typically jobs considered unclean such as grave digging or butchery.
The largest group in medieval society, who undertook the bulk of physical work, most of it related to farming.
The way a person or particular people view some aspect of the past. Perspectives are shaped by prejudices, fears, uncertainties, age, gender and education.
A samurai without a master or lord.
Japan's foreign policy of isolation during the Tokugawa shogunate (1633 to 1853) that forbade Japanese people leaving Japan or foreigners entering it. The penalty was death.
A Japanese medieval warrior who lived by the bushido code and was loyal to his daimyo.
A Tokugawa system that required daimyo to reside in Edo for periods of time, alternating with residence at their own castle.
A ritual suicide common among samurai who felt they had been dishonoured, involving cutting open the belly.
A medieval peasant who worked on the manor of a feudal lord and was bound to that land.
The title given to Japan's top military rulers between the 12th and 19th centuries.
The importance of an event, person or development in the past, judged by how much it changed people's lives or how it helps us understand history today.
One tenth of annual produce or earnings, taken as a contribution for the support of the Catholic Church and clergy.
Doing or saying something that goes against the laws of the king or is seen as a betrayal of the king.
An event or development that leads to a major change in the direction of history.
Under feudalism, a person who offered loyalty and service to a lord in return for protection and the granting of a fief.
A process whereby societies adopt what is considered to be Western culture in areas such as industry, technology, science, education, politics, law and social norms.
